Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Contents 1 Overview 2 Gameplay 2.1 Keepers with Special Powers 2.2 Creepers 2.2.1 Attaching Creepers 2.2.1.1 Special Icons 2.3 Surprises 2.4 Limits 3 End of the Game 4 List of all cards Overview The game starts with just a couple simple rules, then becomes more complex little by little as additional Rule cards are played. At first there will be no way to win - that's what goal cards are for. Each Goal has a different victory condition, but they all require you to collect special cards called Keepers. As soon as someone's collection of Keepers matches the current Goal, they win! Gameplay Place the basic rules (draw 1, play 1) and deal 3 cards to each player. On your turn, draw and play cards as required by the current Rule card(s) If the played card is a Rule card, apply immediately and discard any contradicting rules. example: If there is a Draw 4 Rule card in play and you play a Draw 2 Rule card, the Draw 4 is discarded If you change the number of cards to Draw or Play, this change takes effect immediately. example: If you drew 1 card but play a Draw 3, you immediately draw 2 additional cards example: If you have played 3 cards and play a new Rule Play Four, you must continue playing; if new rule Play 2, since you've already played more than 2, your turn is over If it is a Keeper card, place in your Keeper area of play If it is a Goal card, discard the old goal and replace with the new Goal. If it is an Action, apply it immediately then discard. Some new rules (example: Wormhole) may give optional Actions during your turn; these can (mostly) be used at any point during the turn, before, between or after other, regular actions. After you play the number of cards indicated by the current Play "X" Rule (and activate any extra actions), your turn is over Keepers with Special Powers Some Keepers have special powers that give optional Actions once they are on the table. example: The Scientist may take 1 Keeper per turn from another player; Energy Being, Energy Crystals, or Monolith Creepers These are like Keepers you do not want. Usually Creepers prevent you from winning, but sometimes you actually need them to win. Creepers are kept on the table in front of you in the same area as your Keepers. Creepers cannot be held in your hand. Instead, they automatically go into play. As soon as you draw a Creeper (including as part of your starting hand), you must place it face up in front of you and draw another card. This does NOT count as a "play." You might have to accept several Creepers at once as you draw cards, until you've drawn the required number of non-Creepers and added them to your hand. Note that this is true any time you draw a card, such as during an Action. Attaching Creepers Creepers marked with this icon will become attached to one of your Keepers. If you have no Keepers in play, they will wait patiently until something arrives. Once attached, the two cards are considered a unit until removed from play. It is possible to have more than one Creeper attached to a single Keeper (example: Evil Brain Parasites or Evil Malfunction) Special Icons This version of Fluxx uses the following themed icons: Living Being : This icon is used to label items that are live beings and therefore susceptible to Brain Parasites. Mechanical Device : This icon is used to label items that are equipment and therefore susceptible to Malfunction. Surprises These cards can be played at any time, even when it isn't your turn. community_text:
[Rating: 1/10] Uhm... that's pretty much the opposite of a game I like. Pure randomness and no balance at all. You could even win the game in your first turn...

[Rating: 1/10] I really hate this game.  It is extremely random, so much so that you can't care about the game.  There is no strategy.  It can also take a long time.

[Rating: 1/10] I enjoy random nonsense... to a degree. This game has cards that will cause total analysis paralysis and bloat the game to obscene degrees of length for what is ostensibly a filler game, and if it is aiming for higher, then it is among the most mediocre and boorish experiences money can buy.

[Rating: 1/10] Star Fluxx does have an interesting theme but like the other Fluxx games is highly random and chaotic with goals/cards changing radically from turn to turn. Hard to view this even as a loose tactical game.

[Rating: 1.5/10] MY rating is mostly for the fact that I really do not like this game in the least bit.In my opinion,it simply is not fun whatsoever. I do not understand the love that all the versions of this game receives. I'm sorry, but this is the epitome of a non-game. It can end in less than the time it takes to shuffle the cards, or as long as Twilight Imperium 4. And for a silly card game, that is preposterous. It's all luck. No strategy no tactics, it's up there with Phase 10 and UNO. There are not many games out there that I will straight up refuse to play if someone asks me, but this is one of them. 

[Rating: 2/10] 1. Invite some friends over, one of whom is your tenth- or twelfth-funniest friend, who watches a lot of Star Trek.  2. Deal out a deck of cards to your friends. Whoever gets the four of spades wins.  3. Listen to your friend make jokes the whole time.  4. I just saved you $12. You're welcome.

[Rating: 2/10] It's nice to see Fluxx get redesigned with a more streamlined path to victory, combining clever card play with bonus effects, giving the game an engine to allow players to ramp up their efficiency and--  Nah, I'm just fucking with you.  This is still the same old Fluxx.  1 play: 4 players

[Rating: 2/10] Too random.  Minimal strategy or tactics, it's just a luck-fest and serious lack of fun.  Never need to play this again.

[Rating: 2/10] It's Fluxx in space with no change to mechanices, so it's still Fluxx. You'll like it just as much as you do any other Fluxx variant.

[Rating: 2/10] I'm going to give Fluxx the benefit of a doubt and assume it's wildly different than Star Fluxx, the only version I have played. Star Fluxx is one of the least entertaining things I've played.  I'd jokingly compare Fluxx "just roll a die, highest roll wins" except that game sounds better.  I have to compare Fluxx to another game I love dearly, 1000 Blank White Cards. 1KBWC also has random, unpredictable rules and a chaotic game, so why does it get a pass? [Rating: 2/10] win conditions constantly changing, any plan you make is out the window by the time it's your turn again.......

[Rating: 2/10] The references will please sci-fi fans, but the outcome of any given game is almost entirely based on chance.

[Rating: 2/10] Fluxx is more of a joke than a game. You need a good group to make it really funny though, but then you could play any excellent party game to have fun and laugh.

[Rating: 2/10] I don't know. I guess the randomness works, but it felt more like an activity than a game.
